messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 21-year-old European man, works in social ministry and was married just last year. His life took a dramatic turn when he served as a relief worker in a war zone. The traumatic event that has left lasting marks on his psyche occurred during one of the missions where an explosion rocked the area while he was trying to distribute aid. The memory of that day remains vivid, and it is hard for Mark to believe that such extreme violence actually happened to him. Since returning home, any mention of military topics or hearing shouting in Arabic triggers intense reactions within him. These triggers often lead to nightmares and flashbacks, compelling him to ruminate on how the event could have been prevented if only he had acted differently. This constant rumination is one of his maladaptive strategies, along with staying up very late to avoid falling asleep for fear that he won't wake up from another nightmarish dream. Mark's wife has noticed a significant change in him since he returned. He avoids situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful because the contrast between those moments and his traumatic experiences feels too stark. His memory of the event is so intense that it feels like it’s happening right now rather than something from the past, which makes him relive the terror repeatedly. The memories are exacerbated by his triggers, making it impossible for Mark to function normally at times. For instance, when he hears shouting in Arabic or discusses military topics, he often wakes up during the night to check whether he is safe, driven by a deep-seated belief that strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations pose a threat. This sense of threat from others and his waking alertness only serves to reinforce his memory. He feels as if the danger is always looming, and this heightened state of vigilance makes it difficult for Mark to distinguish between real threats and perceived ones. His fear becomes self-reinforcing; each trigger leads him back into a cycle of rumination and hyper-vigilance. As Mark’s occupation involves interacting with people in various communities, his condition has affected how he performs his duties. He avoids going to certain areas or events where he might encounter triggers that could set off the cycle again. This avoidance behavior has strained his relationships at work, leading him to miss important meetings and community gatherings. What frightens Mark most is the thought of never being able to return to a state of normalcy without these intrusive memories and heightened fears. His maladaptive strategies, like delaying sleep and ruminating about how he could have prevented the event, have only exacerbated his symptoms over time. The cycle feels unbreakable, as each element reinforces the other. Mark finally sought help after realizing that he couldn't manage his condition on his own. He is hoping for relief from the constant fear and terror that plague him daily. His biggest hope is to regain control of his life without the overwhelming sense of threat and the relentless reminders of the event that continue to haunt him.
